newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-B.A.T set for flat Q1 trading.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-B.A.T set for flat Q1 trading.

text.p: Tobacco-to-insurance group B.A.T Industries Plc should report flat profits for its first quarter on Wednesday, but the figures themselves will be overshadowed by investor questions about litigation in the United States.
Analysts expectations for pretax profits range from 544 to 610 million stg, excluding a sale by the group's Canadian associate Imasco, little changed from 590 million last time.

The first quarter 1996 included a 33 million stg profit on the sale of the Chilean food business while the first quarter of this year will include a 50 million profit on the sale by Imasco, of its U.S. savings and loan business.
The first quarter will also bear the 20 million stg cost of the closure of the Berlin cigarette plant and analysts expect a negative exchange rate effect of 25 million stg.
In financial services the continued softness of rates is likely to have affected general insurer Eagle Star, but Allied Dunbar and U.S. insurer Farmers are expected to have made steady progress.

General financial services should show trading profit of some 143 million against 140 million last time, while the life business is forecast to post flat profits of about 118 million. Tobacco should turn in a virtually unchanged operating profit of 355 million, according to analysts forecasts.
But the figures themselves are unlikely to attract much interest with investors and analysts who are focused on the litigation process going on in the United States.
Last week two more states joined the 22 state attorneys general suing major tobacco companies for recovery of Medicaid funds spent to assist patients with tobacco-related illnesses.
The state of Missouri is suing the tobacco industry for targeting children in advertising and for lying to consumers about the addictive nature of nicotine.

Pennsylvania filed a suit against the largest tobacco companies to seek to recover possibly over $1 billion in Medicaid bills the state has paid to treat people suffering from tobacco related illnesses.

Canada's health minister David Dingwall indicated that the litigation problem for the industry is not confined to the United States, by saying he was considering possible lawsuits against tobacco companies to recoup the costs of treating people who suffer from illnesses caused by tobacco.

There is also uncertainty in the investment community over to what extent B.A.T may be covered for legal costs and any compensation it may pay into a settlement scheme by general insurance policies it owns.
B.A.T shares stood 4p lower at 514p in afternoon trade reaching a low for the year of 513p against a year high of 570p.
Industry analysts expect continued volatility in tobacco share prices as speculation about the progress of settlement talks and the litigation timetable in the United States heats up further in June.
The shares slid on Friday after chairman Lord Cairns warned shareholders at the company's annual meeting that if the strength of sterling persists it will hold back profits at a pretax level in 1997.
Analysts said they estimate B.A.T will take a 20 million stg currency hit in the first quarter.
-- Tim Farrand, London Newsroom +44 171 542 6437 Friday, 25 April 1997 14:40:14
